belief: I can never please my parents.
origins: Some parents set standards that keep moving. A good grade is met with “why not an A-plus,” a success is met with silence, and a mistake is remembered for years. Children of such homes often grow into adults who work hard to earn approval that never comes, and who feel on edge around their parents even decades later.
teaches: Paul asks, “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.” The psalmist says, “I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Scripture does call us to honor our father and mother, but honor is not the same as winning their approval. Honor can mean respect, kindness, and care, offered without needing their applause. The Bible also tells fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, which means that impossible standards are a parent’s failing, not a child’s.
self_statements: Nothing I do is ever enough.
They will always find something wrong.
I am a disappointment to them.
If I try harder, maybe they will finally approve.
errors: Assuming I know in advance how they will react.
Insisting that I should be able to win their approval.
Believing I am either pleasing them or failing.
Treating their dissatisfaction as proof of my failure.
questions: When did I first notice that nothing was ever enough?
Is it possible that their dissatisfaction says more about them than about me?
What would pleasing them completely look like, and has it ever been possible?
What is the difference between honoring my parents and needing their approval?
What does God say about me?
What would change if I stopped trying to earn their applause?
truth: I can honor my parents without needing to win their approval. Their standards are not the measure of my worth. God accepts me in Christ, and I can live to please Him and serve people with a free heart.
hw_truths: My worth is not their approval.
I can honor my parents without earning their praise.
Impossible standards are not my fault.
I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
I am free to live to please God.
log: Each week, note one time you honored a parent without seeking approval.
actions: Write what your parents expected and whether anyone could have met it.
Do one kind thing for a parent without hoping for praise.
Before contact, decide in advance how you will respond calmly to criticism.
Say it before a difficult conversation.
prayer: Lord, I have worn myself out trying to please people who are never satisfied. Teach me to honor my parents and to rest in Your approval. Free me from the need to earn what You have already given. Amen.
hw_questions: What does honor look like without approval?
What does God say about me?
What will I say when criticized?
name_example: Sarah can write: “I can honor my parents and still live to please God.”
